title: "Don't say that, Ananda"
hookLine: Ananda finds dependent origination clear; the Buddha says it is deep

lines: ANANDA: DEEP, BUT CLEAR TO ME.
cards: A flat-pack bookshelf comes with one page of instructions. Read once, it looks simple. An hour later, someone is sitting on the floor surrounded by screws.
Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, has heard the teaching again and again.
One day in the market town of Kammasadhamma he comes to the Buddha and says, in effect: it's wonderful how deep this teaching of dependent origination is, and yet to me it seems perfectly clear.
The answer he gets opens the fifteenth Long Discourse.

teach.b: The discourse is the Mahanidana, the great discourse on causes. The Buddha's reply comes twice: don't say that, Ananda, don't say that. This dependent origination is deep, and it looks deep.

It is because people don't understand it, don't penetrate it, that this generation has become like a tangled ball of thread, like a knotted skein, like matted reeds and rushes, and can't get past the round of birth and death.
The warning is aimed at one particular mistake: confusing familiar with understood.
Then, instead of arguing, the Buddha teaches it again, slowly, from the other end. Aging and death have a condition: birth. Birth has a condition: becoming.
And on back through clinging, craving, feeling and contact, until he reaches a strange loop.
Consciousness depends on name-and-form, and name-and-form depends on consciousness, like two sheaves of reeds leaning on each other, to borrow an image from another sutta.
He even walks through craving in the world: because of craving, seeking; because of seeking, gain; and on down to the stick and the knife, quarrels and lies.
One teaching, from the deepest roots of a life to an argument at a family dinner.
Tradition remembers Ananda as the one who carried the discourses home in memory. And here, the one who had heard so much is told: slow down. It is deeper than it looks.

how: Teachers in many Buddhist schools return to dependent origination again and again over years of study, and the Mahanidana Sutta is often studied slowly, link by link, in monastic and lay study groups.

o: the cycle of offerings and their rewards
a chain of fate fixed at birth
arising in dependence, link by link

games.q: "don't say that, Ananda": tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha calls Ananda foolish for his remark
he says 'don't say that' and then teaches it again, carefully.
in DN 15 consciousness and name-and-form depend on each other
the chain loops: each is a condition for the other.
DN 15 traces craving all the way to quarrels and weapons
craving leads to seeking, gain, and on to the stick and the knife.

games.q: your attendant says the hardest thing you teach seems perfectly clear to him. what do you do?
o: praise him: he's ready for something harder.
tell him not to say that, and teach it again from the start.
stay silent and let him find out.
games.why: the Buddha says 'don't say that, Ananda' twice, calls it deep, and then walks him through the links once more.

practice: Choose one thing you're sure you understand, your job, someone close to you, your own temper, the breath itself, and quietly ask: what don't I know about this? Let the question stay open, like a door left ajar.
If the mind says, I already know, smile at it and ask again.

wordCard.voice: Paticcasamuppada. The Buddha's teaching on dependent origination, in the Mahanidana Sutta: it is deep, and it looks deep. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali paticcasamuppada: arising in dependence. the teaching Ananda thought was clear.

carryVoice: Your line: deeper than it looks. Familiar is not the same as understood. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 15 (Mahanidana Sutta), Ananda's remark and the Buddha's reply
Samyutta Nikaya 12.67 (Nalakalapiya Sutta), two sheaves of reeds
